items.title: Circuit Breaker
items.content: Design pattern that stops calling a failing service after a threshold of errors, returning fast and giving the dependency time to recover before retrying.

items.title: gRPC
items.content: High-performance RPC framework by Google using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for fast, strongly-typed, bidirectional service-to-service communication.

items.title: Lazy Loading
items.content: Defer creating or fetching a resource until it is actually needed, reducing initial load time and memory; common for images, modules, and ORM relations.

items.title: TCP Socket
items.content: Endpoint of a reliable, connection-oriented TCP stream identified by IP and port; guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery between two hosts.

items.title: GraphQL
items.content: Query language and runtime for APIs that lets clients request exactly the fields they need from a single endpoint, avoiding over- and under-fetching.

items.title: SQL
items.content: Structured Query Language for relational databases; defines and manipulates data with tables, joins, and transactions enforcing a fixed schema.

items.title: NoSQL
items.content: Family of non-relational databases (document, key-value, column, graph) optimized for scale, flexible schemas, and high write throughput.

items.title: REST API
items.content: Architectural style using stateless HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) on resources identified by URLs, typically exchanging JSON.

items.title: WebSocket
items.content: Full-duplex, persistent TCP connection over a single HTTP upgrade, enabling real-time bidirectional messaging like chat and live feeds.

items.title: Message Queue
items.content: Asynchronous buffer (RabbitMQ, Kafka) that decouples producers from consumers, smoothing load spikes and enabling reliable, retryable delivery.

items.title: Microservices
items.content: Architecture splitting an app into small, independently deployable services that own their data and communicate over the network.

items.title: Monolithic Architecture
items.content: Single deployable unit where all modules share one codebase and process; simple to build but harder to scale and deploy independently.

items.title: Load Balancer
items.content: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to maximize throughput, minimize latency, and avoid overloading any single node.

items.title: CDN
items.content: Content Delivery Network of geographically distributed edge servers that cache static assets close to users for lower latency.

items.title: Caching
items.content: Store frequently accessed data in fast storage (Redis, Memcached) to cut latency and database load; mind invalidation and TTLs.

items.title: ORM
items.content: Object-Relational Mapping maps database tables to objects so you query in code instead of raw SQL; watch for N+1 queries.

items.title: Dependency Injection
items.content: Pass a component's dependencies in from outside instead of constructing them internally, improving testability and decoupling.

items.title: Event-Driven Architecture
items.content: Components communicate by emitting and reacting to events asynchronously, enabling loose coupling and high scalability.

items.title: CI/CD
items.content: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment automate build, test, and release so code changes ship safely and frequently.

items.title: Containerization
items.content: Package an app with its dependencies into a portable, isolated container (Docker) that runs the same everywhere.

items.title: Kubernetes
items.content: Container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, self-healing, and networking of containerized workloads.

items.title: API Gateway
items.content: Single entry point that routes, authenticates, rate-limits, and aggregates requests to backend microservices.

items.title: Rate Limiting
items.content: Cap how many requests a client may make in a window to protect services from abuse and overload (token bucket, leaky bucket).

items.title: Sharding
items.content: Horizontally partition a database across nodes by a shard key so each holds a subset of data, enabling scale beyond one machine.

items.title: Replication
items.content: Keep copies of data across multiple nodes for high availability and read scaling; can be synchronous or asynchronous.

items.title: Indexing
items.content: Database structure (often a B-tree) that speeds up reads on indexed columns at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.

items.title: Deadlock
items.content: Two or more processes wait forever on resources each other holds; prevent with lock ordering, timeouts, or detection.

items.title: ACID vs BASE
items.content: ACID (Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable) favors strong consistency; BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) favors availability and scale.

items.title: Immutable
items.content: An object whose state cannot change after creation; safer for concurrency and caching because no one can mutate it unexpectedly.

items.title: Idempotency
items.content: An operation that produces the same result whether called once or many times; critical for safe API retries (e.g. PUT, DELETE).

items.title: Big O Notation
items.content: Describes how an algorithm's time or space grows with input size (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n^2)) for comparing efficiency.

items.title: Race Condition
items.content: Bug where the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations accessing shared state.

items.title: Memoization
items.content: Cache the results of expensive pure function calls keyed by their arguments so repeats return instantly.

items.title: Pure Function
items.content: A function whose output depends only on its inputs and that causes no side effects, making it predictable and testable.

items.title: Polymorphism
items.content: OOP principle where one interface serves multiple underlying types, so the same call behaves differently per object.

items.title: Recursion
items.content: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on smaller subproblems until reaching a base case.

items.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
items.content: Concurrency structures work to make progress on many tasks; parallelism actually runs them simultaneously on multiple cores.

items.title: Garbage Collection
items.content: Automatic memory management that reclaims objects no longer reachable, freeing developers from manual free() calls.

items.title: Hash Table
items.content: Data structure mapping keys to values via a hash function, giving average O(1) insert and lookup.

items.title: Eventual Consistency
items.content: Distributed model where replicas may differ briefly but converge to the same value once writes stop propagating.

items.title: CAP Theorem
items.content: A distributed store can guarantee only two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance at once.

items.title: Stateless vs Stateful
items.content: Stateless services keep no client context between requests (easy to scale); stateful ones retain session data.

items.title: Webhook
items.content: User-defined HTTP callback fired by an event, letting one system push real-time data to another instead of polling.

items.title: OAuth 2.0
items.content: Authorization framework that grants apps limited access to user resources via tokens without sharing passwords.

items.title: JWT
items.content: JSON Web Token: a signed, self-contained token carrying claims, used for stateless authentication between parties.

items.title: CORS
items.content: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: browser mechanism using HTTP headers to allow or block requests across different origins.

items.title: XSS
items.content: Cross-Site Scripting: injecting malicious scripts into pages viewed by others; prevent by escaping output and using CSP.

items.title: SQL Injection
items.content: Attack that injects malicious SQL via unsanitized input; prevent with parameterized queries and ORMs.

items.title: CSRF
items.content: Cross-Site Request Forgery tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending unwanted requests; defend with anti-CSRF tokens.

items.title: Hashing vs Encryption
items.content: Hashing is one-way and used for integrity/passwords; encryption is reversible with a key and used for confidentiality.

items.title: TLS/SSL
items.content: Cryptographic protocol that encrypts data in transit and authenticates servers, powering HTTPS.

items.title: DNS
items.content: Domain Name System translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses through a distributed hierarchy of servers.

items.title: HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
items.content: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP to remove head-of-line blocking.

items.title: Proxy vs Reverse Proxy
items.content: A forward proxy represents clients to the internet; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers handling routing, TLS, and caching.

items.title: Pagination
items.content: Split large result sets into pages (offset or cursor based) to limit payload size and improve performance.

items.title: Debouncing vs Throttling
items.content: Debounce waits for a pause before firing; throttle limits firing to once per interval—both tame noisy events.

items.title: Virtual DOM
items.content: In-memory representation of the UI that frameworks diff against to apply minimal real DOM updates efficiently.

items.title: Tree Shaking
items.content: Build-time elimination of unused code (dead exports) to shrink JavaScript bundle size.

items.title: Blue-Green Deployment
items.content: Run two identical production environments and switch traffic to the new one for zero-downtime releases and instant rollback.

items.title: Canary Release
items.content: Roll out a change to a small subset of users first, monitor, then expand—limiting blast radius of bugs.

items.title: Infrastructure as Code
items.content: Manage and provision infrastructure through declarative files (Terraform) versioned like application code.

items.title: Observability
items.content: Ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs—logs, metrics, and traces (the three pillars).

items.title: Saga Pattern
items.content: Manage distributed transactions across microservices as a sequence of local steps with compensating actions on failure.

items.title: CQRS
items.content: Command Query Responsibility Segregation separates read and write models so each can be optimized and scaled independently.

items.title: Event Sourcing
items.content: Persist state as an immutable log of events rather than current values, enabling full history and replay.

items.title: Backpressure
items.content: Mechanism for a consumer to signal a fast producer to slow down, preventing buffer overflow in streams.

items.title: Connection Pooling
items.content: Reuse a fixed set of open database connections across requests instead of opening one per query.

items.title: Normalization vs Denormalization
items.content: Normalization removes redundancy for integrity; denormalization duplicates data to speed reads.

items.title: Write code for humans
items.content: Optimize for readability first—code is read far more often than it is written. Clear names beat clever one-liners.

items.title: Commit small and often
items.content: Make focused commits with clear messages so history is easy to review, revert, and bisect.

items.title: Fail fast and loud
items.content: Validate inputs early and throw clear errors instead of letting bad state propagate silently.

items.title: Don't optimize prematurely
items.content: Make it work, make it right, then make it fast—measure with a profiler before optimizing.

items.title: DRY principle
items.content: Don't Repeat Yourself: extract duplicated logic into one source of truth to ease maintenance.

items.title: KISS principle
items.content: Keep It Simple, Stupid: prefer the simplest solution that works; complexity is a long-term cost.

items.title: YAGNI
items.content: You Aren't Gonna Need It: don't build features on speculation—add them when actually required.

items.title: Use meaningful names
items.content: Name variables and functions for intent, not type; a good name removes the need for a comment.

items.title: Boy Scout Rule
items.content: Leave the code cleaner than you found it—small continual refactors prevent rot.

items.title: Read the error message
items.content: The stack trace usually points to the exact line and cause—read it fully before guessing.

items.title: Rubber duck debugging
items.content: Explain your code line by line to an inanimate object; articulating it often reveals the bug.

items.title: Automate repetitive tasks
items.content: If you do something manually more than twice, script it—save time and reduce human error.

items.title: Back up before you delete
items.content: Always snapshot or branch before destructive operations; recovery is cheaper than regret.

items.title: Write tests for bugs
items.content: When you fix a bug, add a test that reproduces it so it can never silently return.

items.title: Prefer composition over inheritance
items.content: Build behavior by combining small parts rather than deep class hierarchies that are rigid and fragile.

items.title: Docker
items.content: Platform that packages applications into lightweight, portable containers sharing the host kernel for consistent runs everywhere.

items.title: Git
items.content: Distributed version control system tracking code history, enabling branching, merging, and collaboration.

items.title: Postman
items.content: API client for building, testing, and documenting HTTP requests and automated test collections.

items.title: Redis
items.content: In-memory key-value store used for caching, sessions, queues, and pub/sub with optional persistence.

items.title: Terraform
items.content: Infrastructure-as-Code tool that provisions cloud resources declaratively across many providers.

items.title: Nginx
items.content: High-performance web server and reverse proxy handling static files, load balancing, and TLS termination.

items.title: Kafka
items.content: Distributed event-streaming platform for high-throughput, durable, ordered message logs and real-time pipelines.

items.title: Prometheus
items.content: Time-series monitoring system that scrapes metrics and powers alerting, often paired with Grafana dashboards.

items.title: Wireshark
items.content: Network protocol analyzer that captures and inspects packets to debug connectivity and security issues.

items.title: VS Code
items.content: Lightweight, extensible code editor with debugging, Git integration, and a vast extension ecosystem.

items.title: React
items.content: Declarative JavaScript library for building component-based user interfaces with a virtual DOM and hooks.

items.title: Node.js
items.content: JavaScript runtime built on V8 with a non-blocking event loop, ideal for scalable I/O-bound network apps.

items.title: Spring Boot
items.content: Opinionated Java framework that auto-configures production-ready apps with minimal boilerplate.

items.title: Flutter
items.content: Google's UI toolkit for building natively compiled mobile, web, and desktop apps from one Dart codebase.

items.title: Django
items.content: Batteries-included Python web framework with an ORM, admin, and security defaults for rapid development.

items.title: Express.js
items.content: Minimal, unopinionated Node.js web framework for building APIs and servers with middleware.

items.title: TensorFlow
items.content: End-to-end open-source platform for building and training machine learning and deep learning models.

items.title: Next.js
items.content: React framework offering server-side rendering, static generation, routing, and full-stack APIs.

items.title: Machine Learning
items.content: Field where algorithms learn patterns from data to make predictions without being explicitly programmed.

items.title: Neural Network
items.content: Model of interconnected layers of weighted nodes that learns complex patterns via backpropagation.

items.title: Overfitting
items.content: When a model memorizes training data and noise, performing well in training but poorly on new data.

items.title: Embedding
items.content: Dense vector representation of data (words, images) capturing semantic similarity for ML and search.

items.title: LLM
items.content: Large Language Model trained on massive text to generate and understand human language (e.g. GPT, Claude).

items.title: RAG
items.content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds an LLM's answers in documents fetched from a knowledge base at query time.

items.title: Prompt Engineering
items.content: Crafting and structuring inputs to guide an LLM toward accurate, useful, and consistent outputs.

items.title: Vector Database
items.content: Database that stores embeddings and performs fast nearest-neighbor similarity search (Pinecone, pgvector).

items.title: Set up a Git repo
items.content: Run git init, create a .gitignore, git add ., then git commit -m 'init'. Add a remote with git remote add origin <url> and git push -u origin main.

items.title: Dockerize a Node app
items.content: Write a Dockerfile FROM node, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY source, EXPOSE the port, CMD npm start. Build with docker build -t app . and run docker run -p 3000:3000 app.

items.title: Build a REST API
items.content: Define resources and routes, map HTTP verbs to CRUD, validate input, return proper status codes, document with OpenAPI, and add auth plus pagination.

items.title: Add Redis caching
items.content: Connect a Redis client, check the cache before hitting the DB (cache-aside), store results with a TTL, and invalidate keys on writes to avoid stale data.

items.title: Deploy with CI/CD
items.content: Add a pipeline that on push installs deps, runs lint and tests, builds an artifact or image, then deploys to staging and promotes to production on approval.

items.title: Write your first unit test
items.content: Pick a pure function, arrange inputs, act by calling it, and assert the expected output. Cover edge cases and run tests in your CI pipeline.

items.title: 12-Factor App
items.content: A methodology of twelve principles (config in env, stateless processes, logs as streams) for building portable, scalable cloud-native apps.

items.title: HTTP Status Codes
items.content: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (400 bad request, 401 unauth, 403 forbidden, 404 not found), 5xx server error (500, 503).

items.title: Semantic Versioning
items.content: Version as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes.

items.title: Git Branching Strategy
items.content: Conventions like Git Flow or trunk-based development that define how teams branch, review, and merge to ship safely.

items.title: OWASP Top 10
items.content: Standard awareness list of the most critical web security risks (injection, broken auth, XSS) every developer should defend against.

items.title: Test each feature when done
items.content: Write unit tests right after finishing a feature while the logic is fresh, locking in behavior before moving on.

items.title: Test with big data
items.content: Verify your code handles large datasets—check pagination, memory use, and query time, not just a few happy-path rows.

items.title: Handle all screen sizes
items.content: Check screen height and width; design responsive layouts that adapt to small phones, tablets, and large displays.

items.title: Focus on performance early
items.content: Avoid nested loops, reduce database round-trips, and cache hot data from the start—late optimization is costly.

items.title: Validate all inputs
items.content: Handle emojis, empty strings, ranges, required vs optional, and domain rules. Never trust client input.

items.title: Sanitize for security
items.content: Sanitize and escape inputs to block SQL injection, XSS, and CSRF; use parameterized queries and CSP.

items.title: Give AI full context
items.content: When prompting AI, share project structure, purpose, stack, and constraints so suggestions actually fit your codebase.

items.title: Pin versions and stack
items.content: Always state language, framework, and exact package versions to AI and in configs to avoid dependency conflicts.

items.title: Keep logs clear
items.content: Make error messages and logs descriptive and actionable so future-you can diagnose issues quickly.

items.title: Ask AI for real examples
items.content: Request concrete input/output examples of the result you want so the AI matches your exact expectations.

items.title: Remove dead code
items.content: Delete unused functions, variables, and imports—dead code adds noise, confusion, and maintenance burden.

items.title: User-friendly error messages
items.content: Show users plain, helpful messages with next steps, not raw stack traces or cryptic codes.

items.title: Document every function
items.content: Write a docstring or JSDoc per function describing params, return, and side effects for easier reuse and onboarding.

items.title: Pick the right storage
items.content: Choose deliberately among SQLite, local files, async storage, and an online DB based on size, sync, and persistence needs.

items.title: Check CORS for APIs
items.content: When calling an API from the browser, confirm CORS headers allow your origin or requests will be blocked.

items.title: Rate-limit your API
items.content: Throttle requests per client to protect against abuse, runaway costs, and accidental overload.

items.title: Version your API
items.content: Version APIs and projects (v1, v2) so you can evolve without breaking existing clients.

items.title: Offload heavy work
items.content: Run slow or heavy tasks (emails, reports, image processing) in background jobs so requests stay fast.

items.title: Update deps carefully
items.content: Keep dependencies current for security, but test thoroughly before upgrading to catch breaking changes.

items.title: Watch for memory leaks
items.content: Profile for memory leaks and remove unused event listeners, timers, and subscriptions that pile up.

items.title: Externalize strings & use enums
items.content: Move user-facing text into a strings file and replace magic values with enums for clarity and localization.

items.title: Handle null safely
items.content: Always guard against null, undefined, and nil with checks, defaults, or optional chaining to avoid crashes.

items.title: Lazy-load large parts
items.content: Defer loading big components or datasets until needed to speed up initial render and save memory.

items.title: Compress assets
items.content: Compress and resize images and minify static assets to cut bandwidth and load time.

items.title: Use logging levels
items.content: Apply debug/info/warn/error levels and enable verbose debug output only in developer mode.

items.title: Monitor with metrics
items.content: Track CPU, memory, and DB usage in production with metrics and alerts to catch issues before users do.

items.title: Use UUIDs when needed
items.content: Prefer UUIDs over sequential IDs when guessable or enumerable IDs would be a security or privacy risk.

items.title: Wrap external calls
items.content: Use circuit breakers and timeouts around external services so one failing dependency can't cascade.

items.title: Store time in UTC
items.content: Persist all timestamps in UTC and convert to local time only at the UI layer to avoid timezone bugs.

items.title: Automate rollback
items.content: Set up automatic rollback so a failed deployment reverts to the last healthy version without manual scramble.

items.title: Set CSP headers
items.content: Add a Content-Security-Policy header to restrict which sources can load scripts and assets, mitigating XSS.

items.title: Plan for localization
items.content: Support multiple languages, currencies, and date formats from the start instead of hard-coding one locale.

items.title: Stream large files
items.content: Stream big uploads and downloads instead of loading them fully into memory to prevent OOM crashes.

items.title: Add a splash screen
items.content: Show an intro/splash screen while initial data loads so the app feels responsive instead of frozen.

items.title: Use safe config defaults
items.content: Default configuration to the secure, least-exposed option so a forgotten setting never leaks data.

items.title: Serve static via CDN
items.content: Separate static assets from dynamic content and serve them through a CDN for speed and lower server load.

items.title: Review algorithmic complexity
items.content: Inspect hot paths for O(n^2) or worse and replace with better data structures or algorithms.

items.title: Test third-party fallbacks
items.content: Simulate missing third-party services or network failures and confirm graceful fallbacks instead of total breakage.

items.title: Test edge cases
items.content: Cover empty arrays, zero values, nulls, and boundaries—most bugs live at the edges, not the happy path.

items.title: Use sanitization libraries
items.content: Rely on vetted input-sanitization libraries instead of hand-rolled checks that miss attack vectors.

items.title: Vet third-party libraries
items.content: Audit dependencies for known vulnerabilities, license, and maintenance before adding them to your project.

items.title: Validate formats
items.content: Verify email, phone, and URL formats—and where possible their real existence—before persisting them.

items.title: Always keep backups
items.content: Maintain regular, tested backups of data and config so you can recover from corruption, deletion, or disaster.

items.title: Never commit secrets
items.content: Keep API keys, passwords, and tokens out of source control; use environment variables or a secrets manager.

items.title: Use environment variables
items.content: Store config that differs per environment (URLs, keys, flags) in env vars, not hard-coded in the source.

items.title: Write a good README
items.content: Document setup, run, and deploy steps so anyone—including future you—can start the project in minutes.

items.title: Use a .gitignore
items.content: Exclude build artifacts, node_modules, and secrets from version control to keep the repo clean and safe.

items.title: Prefer immutability
items.content: Avoid mutating shared data; return new values instead to prevent subtle bugs in concurrent or reactive code.

items.title: Handle loading and error states
items.content: In UIs, always design for loading, empty, and error states—not just the happy path with data present.

items.title: Use transactions for related writes
items.content: Wrap multi-step database writes in a transaction so they all succeed or all roll back, preserving integrity.

items.title: Avoid N+1 queries
items.content: Watch for ORM loops that fire one query per row; use eager loading or joins to fetch in a single query.

items.title: Set timeouts on requests
items.content: Always set timeouts for network and DB calls so a hung dependency can't freeze your whole service.

items.title: Retry with backoff
items.content: Retry transient failures using exponential backoff and jitter instead of hammering a struggling service.

items.title: Make operations idempotent
items.content: Design writes so repeating them is safe, letting clients retry without creating duplicates.

items.title: Paginate large lists
items.content: Never return unbounded result sets; page or limit them to protect memory, bandwidth, and the database.

items.title: Index your queries
items.content: Add database indexes for columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY—but don't over-index and slow writes.

items.title: Profile before optimizing
items.content: Measure with a profiler to find the real bottleneck instead of guessing and optimizing the wrong code.

items.title: Keep functions small
items.content: A function should do one thing; if it needs a comment to explain sections, split it into smaller functions.

items.title: Avoid magic numbers
items.content: Replace unexplained literals with named constants so their meaning and intent are obvious.

items.title: Review your own PR first
items.content: Read your diff before requesting review—catch debug logs, typos, and leftovers reviewers shouldn't have to.

items.title: Use feature branches
items.content: Develop each feature on its own branch and merge via pull request to keep main stable and reviewable.

items.title: Write meaningful commit messages
items.content: Explain what changed and why in the commit body; future debugging via git blame will thank you.

items.title: Fail closed for security
items.content: When an auth or permission check errors, deny access by default rather than letting requests through.

items.title: Hash passwords properly
items.content: Never store plaintext passwords; hash with a slow, salted algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2.

items.title: Principle of least privilege
items.content: Grant users, services, and tokens only the minimum permissions they need to do their job.

items.title: Cache invalidation strategy
items.content: Decide upfront how cached data expires (TTL, event-based) to avoid serving stale results.

items.title: Debounce expensive UI calls
items.content: Debounce search-as-you-type and resize handlers so you don't fire heavy work on every keystroke or pixel.

items.title: Test on real devices
items.content: Emulators lie—test performance, gestures, and network on actual low-end devices users really have.

items.title: Plan for offline mode
items.content: Handle no-connectivity gracefully with caching, queued actions, and clear offline indicators.

items.title: Use semantic HTML and a11y
items.content: Use proper tags, labels, and ARIA so the app works with screen readers and keyboard navigation.

items.title: Measure before scaling
items.content: Confirm you actually have a bottleneck with metrics before adding servers, caches, or complexity.

items.title: Keep one source of truth
items.content: Avoid storing the same data in multiple places that can drift; derive it or reference a single owner.

items.title: Automate your tests in CI
items.content: Run the full test suite on every push so regressions are caught before they reach main or production.

items.title: Log with correlation IDs
items.content: Attach a request/trace ID to every log line so you can follow one request across services.

items.title: Clean up resources
items.content: Always close files, sockets, and DB connections (use finally / context managers) to avoid leaks.

items.title: Validate on the server too
items.content: Client-side validation is for UX only; always re-validate on the server since clients can be bypassed.

items.title: Prefer explicit over clever
items.content: Write obvious code over clever tricks; the next maintainer (often you) values clarity over showing off.

items.title: Document your decisions
items.content: Record why you chose an approach (ADR or comments) so future changes don't undo it unknowingly.

items.title: MVC
items.content: Model-View-Controller pattern separating data (model), UI (view), and logic (controller) for organized, testable apps.

items.title: SOLID Principles
items.content: Five OOP design rules—Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion—for flexible, maintainable code.

items.title: TDD
items.content: Test-Driven Development: write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor (red-green-refactor) for reliable, well-designed code.

items.title: Separation of Concerns
items.content: Design principle of dividing a system into distinct sections that each handle one responsibility, reducing coupling.

items.title: Domain-Driven Design
items.content: Model software around the business domain using a shared ubiquitous language between developers and domain experts.

items.title: Content Security Policy
items.content: Browser security header that whitelists trusted sources for scripts, styles, and media to mitigate XSS and injection.

items.title: UUID
items.content: Universally Unique Identifier: a 128-bit ID generated to be globally unique without a central authority, safe from enumeration.

items.title: Pair Programming
items.content: Two developers work at one workstation—one drives, one reviews—sharing knowledge and catching defects early.

items.title: Code Review
items.content: Systematic peer examination of code before merge to catch bugs, share context, and uphold standards.

items.title: Agile
items.content: Iterative development emphasizing collaboration, customer feedback, and adapting to change via Scrum or Kanban.

items.title: Feature Flag
items.content: Toggle that turns functionality on or off at runtime without redeploying, enabling safe rollouts and A/B tests.

items.title: Graceful Degradation
items.content: Design so the app still provides core functionality when a feature, service, or network is unavailable.

items.title: Memory Leak
items.content: Memory that is allocated but never released, gradually exhausting resources until the app slows or crashes.

items.title: Thread vs Process
items.content: A process is an isolated program with its own memory; threads run concurrently inside a process sharing its memory.

items.title: Mutex vs Semaphore
items.content: A mutex allows one thread into a critical section; a semaphore permits a fixed number—both coordinate shared access.

items.title: JavaScript
items.content: Dynamic, interpreted language of the web that runs in browsers and on servers (Node.js); event-driven and prototype-based.

items.title: TypeScript
items.content: Typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to JS, adding static types, interfaces, and generics to catch errors early.

items.title: Python
items.content: Readable, versatile language popular for AI/ML, scripting, web, and automation thanks to a huge ecosystem.

items.title: Scalability
items.content: A system's ability to handle growing load by scaling vertically (bigger machines) or horizontally (more machines).

items.title: Latency vs Throughput
items.content: Latency is the time for one request to complete; throughput is how many requests are handled per unit time. Optimize both.

items.title: High Availability
items.content: Designing systems to stay operational with minimal downtime, measured in nines (99.9%, 99.99%) via redundancy and failover.

items.title: Fault Tolerance
items.content: The ability of a system to keep working correctly even when components fail, through redundancy and graceful handling.

items.title: Consistent Hashing
items.content: Hashing technique that distributes keys across nodes so adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys.

items.title: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
items.content: Horizontal scaling adds more machines; vertical scaling adds more power to one machine. Horizontal scales further but is more complex.

items.title: Bloom Filter
items.content: Space-efficient probabilistic structure that tells you if an element is definitely absent or possibly present—no false negatives.

items.title: Write-Ahead Log
items.content: Durability technique where changes are appended to a log before being applied, so a crash can be recovered by replaying it.

items.title: Leader Election
items.content: Process by which distributed nodes agree on a single coordinator (leader) to avoid conflicts, e.g. via Raft or Paxos.

items.title: Quorum
items.content: Minimum number of nodes that must agree on a read or write for it to be considered successful in a distributed system.

items.title: Heartbeat
items.content: Periodic signal a node sends to prove it is alive; missing heartbeats trigger failover or rebalancing.

items.title: Two-Phase Commit
items.content: Distributed transaction protocol where a coordinator asks all nodes to prepare, then commit, ensuring atomicity across services.

items.title: Idempotency Key
items.content: Unique client-supplied key letting a server detect and ignore duplicate requests, making retries safe.

items.title: Read Replica
items.content: A copy of a database that serves read traffic to offload the primary and scale reads horizontally.

items.title: Polling vs Long Polling vs SSE
items.content: Polling repeatedly asks for updates; long polling holds the request open; Server-Sent Events stream one-way updates over HTTP.

items.title: Serverless
items.content: Cloud model where you run functions without managing servers; the provider scales and bills per execution (e.g. AWS Lambda).

items.title: Cold Start
items.content: Latency spike when a serverless function or container starts from scratch before it can handle a request.

items.title: Blob/Object Storage
items.content: Storage for large unstructured files (images, video, backups) via APIs, e.g. S3—cheap, durable, and scalable.

items.title: Data Lake vs Data Warehouse
items.content: A data lake stores raw data of any format; a warehouse stores cleaned, structured data optimized for analytics queries.

items.title: ETL
items.content: Extract, Transform, Load: pipeline that pulls data from sources, reshapes it, and loads it into a destination for analytics.

items.title: Distributed Cache
items.content: Cache spread across multiple nodes (e.g. Redis Cluster) so cached data scales and survives single-node failures.

items.title: WebRTC
items.content: Browser API and protocol for real-time peer-to-peer audio, video, and data without plugins.

items.title: Array
items.content: Contiguous block of memory giving O(1) indexed access; fixed or dynamic size, the most fundamental structure.

items.title: Linked List
items.content: Sequence of nodes each pointing to the next, allowing O(1) insertion/removal but O(n) lookup.

items.title: Stack
items.content: Last-In-First-Out structure supporting push and pop; powers call stacks, undo, and DFS.

items.title: Queue
items.content: First-In-First-Out structure with enqueue and dequeue; used for buffering, scheduling, and BFS.

items.title: Binary Search Tree
items.content: Ordered tree where left < node < right, giving O(log n) search, insert, and delete when balanced.

items.title: Heap
items.content: Tree-based priority structure giving O(log n) insert and O(1) peek of the min or max; backs priority queues.

items.title: Graph
items.content: Set of nodes connected by edges modeling networks, maps, and dependencies; traversed with BFS/DFS.

items.title: Trie
items.content: Prefix tree storing strings by character, enabling fast autocomplete and prefix search.

items.title: Hash Map
items.content: Key-value structure using a hash function for average O(1) insert and lookup; watch for collisions.

items.title: Binary Search
items.content: Algorithm that finds an item in a sorted array in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search range.

items.title: Dynamic Programming
items.content: Solve complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and caching results to avoid recomputation.

items.title: Greedy Algorithm
items.content: Make the locally optimal choice at each step hoping for a global optimum; fast but not always correct.

items.title: Singleton Pattern
items.content: Creational pattern ensuring a class has only one instance with a global access point; use sparingly.

items.title: Factory Pattern
items.content: Creational pattern defining an interface for creating objects while letting subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

items.title: Builder Pattern
items.content: Creational pattern that constructs complex objects step by step, separating construction from representation.

items.title: Observer Pattern
items.content: Behavioral pattern where subjects notify a list of observers of state changes—the basis of pub/sub and reactivity.

items.title: Strategy Pattern
items.content: Behavioral pattern that encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface, selectable at runtime.

items.title: Adapter Pattern
items.content: Structural pattern that wraps one interface so an incompatible class can be used where another is expected.

items.title: Decorator Pattern
items.content: Structural pattern that dynamically adds responsibilities to an object without subclassing.

items.title: Facade Pattern
items.content: Structural pattern providing a simplified interface to a complex subsystem, hiding its internals.

items.title: Proxy Pattern
items.content: Structural pattern providing a placeholder that controls access to another object (lazy load, caching, access control).

items.title: Repository Pattern
items.content: Abstracts data access behind a collection-like interface so business logic doesn't depend on the storage details.

items.title: Process vs Thread
items.content: A process is an isolated program with its own memory; threads share a process's memory and run concurrently.

items.title: Context Switch
items.content: The OS saving one task's state and loading another's to share the CPU; frequent switches add overhead.

items.title: Virtual Memory
items.content: OS abstraction giving each process its own large address space, paging data between RAM and disk as needed.

items.title: OSI Model
items.content: Seven-layer conceptual model (Physical to Application) describing how data moves through a network.

items.title: TCP vs UDP
items.content: TCP is reliable, ordered, and connection-based; UDP is fast, connectionless, and lossy—good for streaming and games.

items.title: IP Address & Subnet
items.content: An IP uniquely identifies a host on a network; a subnet mask defines which portion is network vs host.

items.title: NAT
items.content: Network Address Translation maps private internal IPs to a public IP, letting many devices share one address.

items.title: Three-Way Handshake
items.content: TCP connection setup: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK—establishes synchronized sequence numbers before data flows.

items.title: HTTPS Handshake
items.content: TLS negotiation where client and server agree on ciphers and exchange keys to encrypt the session.

items.title: DNS Resolution
items.content: Process of translating a domain name to an IP via recursive and authoritative name servers, often cached.

items.title: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS
items.content: IaaS rents raw infrastructure, PaaS provides a managed platform to deploy apps, SaaS delivers ready software.

items.title: Autoscaling
items.content: Automatically adding or removing compute capacity based on load metrics to balance cost and performance.

items.title: Service Mesh
items.content: Infrastructure layer (e.g. Istio) handling service-to-service traffic, security, and observability via sidecars.

items.title: GitOps
items.content: Operate infrastructure and deployments by treating a Git repo as the single source of truth, auto-syncing the cluster.

items.title: Immutable Infrastructure
items.content: Replace servers with new images on every change instead of patching them in place, ensuring consistency.

items.title: Secrets Management
items.content: Securely storing, rotating, and accessing credentials (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) instead of hard-coding them.

items.title: Use a linter and formatter
items.content: Adopt automated linting and formatting (Prettier, Black) so the team stops arguing about style and catches issues early.

items.title: Design the API before coding
items.content: Agree on endpoints, payloads, and errors first so frontend and backend can build in parallel against a contract.

items.title: Make illegal states unrepresentable
items.content: Model your types so invalid combinations can't even be constructed, eliminating whole classes of bugs.

items.title: Prefer early returns
items.content: Return or throw on invalid cases early to avoid deep nesting and keep the happy path flat and readable.

items.title: Cache at the right layer
items.content: Decide whether to cache in the browser, CDN, app, or database—each layer trades freshness for speed differently.

items.title: Graceful shutdown
items.content: On shutdown, stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, and close connections so you don't drop data.

items.title: Use health checks
items.content: Expose liveness and readiness endpoints so orchestrators can restart or route around unhealthy instances.

items.title: Avoid premature abstraction
items.content: Wait for the third repetition before abstracting; the wrong abstraction is costlier than a little duplication.

items.title: Write idempotent migrations
items.content: Make database migrations safe to re-run and reversible so deployments and rollbacks don't corrupt schema.

items.title: Set resource limits
items.content: Cap CPU and memory for containers and queries so one runaway process can't starve everything else.

items.title: Test the unhappy path
items.content: Deliberately test timeouts, malformed data, and failures—real systems break at the edges, not the demo path.

items.title: Keep secrets out of logs
items.content: Scrub tokens, passwords, and PII before logging so sensitive data doesn't leak into log aggregators.

items.title: Version your database schema
items.content: Track schema changes in versioned migration files in source control so every environment stays in sync.

items.title: Prefer UTC and ISO 8601
items.content: Store and exchange dates in UTC using ISO 8601 strings to avoid timezone and parsing ambiguity.

items.title: Limit blast radius
items.content: Isolate failures with bulkheads, timeouts, and circuit breakers so one bad component can't take down the whole system.

items.title: Kibana
items.content: Visualization and exploration UI for Elasticsearch—search logs, build dashboards, and analyze data.

items.title: Ansible
items.content: Agentless automation tool for configuration management, app deployment, and orchestration via YAML playbooks.

items.title: Helm
items.content: Package manager for Kubernetes that templates and versions app deployments as reusable charts.

items.title: GitLab CI

items.title: Playwright
items.content: Modern end-to-end testing framework that automates Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with auto-waiting.

items.title: Cypress
items.content: Developer-friendly end-to-end testing tool for web apps with time-travel debugging and live reload.

items.title: Storybook
items.content: UI workshop for building, documenting, and testing components in isolation across frameworks.

items.title: Pytest
items.content: Powerful, concise Python testing framework with fixtures, parametrization, and rich plugins.

items.title: OWASP ZAP
items.content: Open-source web app security scanner for finding vulnerabilities like XSS and injection during testing.

items.title: k6
items.content: Developer-centric load-testing tool that scripts performance tests in JavaScript to find bottlenecks.

items.title: Datadog
items.content: Cloud monitoring and observability platform unifying metrics, traces, logs, and alerts.

items.title: Prisma
items.content: Next-generation TypeScript/Node ORM with type-safe queries, migrations, and a visual data browser.

items.title: git clone
items.content: Copy a remote repository to your machine: `git clone <url>`. Add a folder name to clone into a specific directory.

items.title: git status
items.content: Show the working tree state—staged, unstaged, and untracked files: `git status`.

items.title: git add
items.content: Stage changes for the next commit: `git add <file>` or `git add .` for everything.

items.title: git commit
items.content: Record staged changes: `git commit -m "message"`. Use `--amend` to edit the last commit.

items.title: git push
items.content: Upload local commits to the remote: `git push origin <branch>`. Use `-u` to set upstream the first time.

items.title: git pull
items.content: Fetch and merge changes from the remote into your branch: `git pull`.

items.title: git branch
items.content: List, create, or delete branches: `git branch` lists, `git branch <name>` creates, `-d` deletes.

items.title: git checkout / switch
items.content: Move between branches: `git switch <branch>` (or `git checkout`). Add `-b` to create and switch.

items.title: git merge
items.content: Combine another branch into the current one: `git merge <branch>`. Resolve conflicts if they arise.

items.title: git rebase
items.content: Reapply commits on top of another base to keep history linear: `git rebase <branch>`. Avoid on shared branches.

items.title: git log
items.content: Show commit history: `git log --oneline --graph --all` for a compact, visual view.

items.title: git stash
items.content: Temporarily shelve uncommitted changes: `git stash`, then `git stash pop` to restore them.

items.title: git reset
items.content: Undo staging or commits: `git reset <file>` unstages; `git reset --hard <commit>` discards changes.

items.title: git revert
items.content: Create a new commit that undoes a previous one: `git revert <commit>`—safe for shared history.

items.title: git cherry-pick
items.content: Apply a specific commit from another branch onto the current one: `git cherry-pick <commit>`.

items.title: git diff
items.content: Show changes between commits, branches, or the working tree: `git diff` or `git diff <a> <b>`.

items.title: git remote
items.content: Manage remote repositories: `git remote -v` lists them, `git remote add origin <url>` adds one.

items.title: git fetch
items.content: Download remote changes without merging: `git fetch`—then review before integrating.

items.title: git tag
items.content: Mark a commit, usually a release: `git tag v1.0.0` and `git push --tags` to publish.

items.title: git blame
items.content: Show who last changed each line of a file: `git blame <file>`—handy for tracking down a change.

items.title: ls
items.content: List directory contents: `ls -la` shows hidden files and details in long format.

items.title: cd
items.content: Change directory: `cd <path>`; `cd ..` goes up, `cd ~` goes home, `cd -` returns to the previous dir.

items.title: grep
items.content: Search text with patterns: `grep -rin "pattern" .` searches recursively, case-insensitive, with line numbers.

items.title: find
items.content: Locate files by name, type, or age: `find . -name "*.log" -mtime +7` finds week-old logs.

items.title: chmod
items.content: Change file permissions: `chmod +x script.sh` makes a script executable; `755` sets rwxr-xr-x.

items.title: chown
items.content: Change file owner and group: `chown user:group file`—often needed after copying or deploying.

items.title: ps & top
items.content: `ps aux` lists running processes; `top` or `htop` shows live CPU and memory usage.

items.title: kill
items.content: Terminate a process by PID: `kill <pid>`; `kill -9` forces it. `pkill <name>` kills by name.

items.title: tar
items.content: Archive and compress files: `tar -czf out.tar.gz dir/` to create, `-xzf` to extract.

items.title: curl
items.content: Transfer data over HTTP and more: `curl -X POST -d '{...}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' <url>`.

items.title: ssh
items.content: Securely connect to a remote machine: `ssh user@host`; add `-i key.pem` for a specific key.

items.title: scp & rsync
items.content: Copy files to/from remote hosts: `scp file user@host:/path`; `rsync -avz` syncs efficiently.

items.title: df & du
items.content: `df -h` shows disk space per filesystem; `du -sh *` shows the size of each item in a directory.

items.title: sed & awk
items.content: Stream-edit and process text: `sed 's/old/new/g'` replaces; `awk '{print $1}'` extracts columns.

items.title: export
items.content: Set an environment variable for the session: `export API_KEY=xyz`; persist it in your shell profile.

items.title: docker build
items.content: Build an image from a Dockerfile: `docker build -t myapp:latest .`.

items.title: docker run
items.content: Start a container: `docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web myapp` runs detached with a port mapping.

items.title: docker ps & logs
items.content: `docker ps` lists running containers; `docker logs -f <id>` streams a container's logs.

items.title: docker exec
items.content: Run a command in a running container: `docker exec -it <id> sh` opens an interactive shell.

items.title: docker compose up
items.content: Start a multi-container app defined in docker-compose.yml: `docker compose up -d`.

items.title: docker images & prune
items.content: `docker images` lists images; `docker system prune -a` reclaims space from unused data.

items.title: kubectl get
items.content: List cluster resources: `kubectl get pods -A` shows pods across all namespaces.

items.title: kubectl apply
items.content: Create or update resources from a manifest: `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`.

items.title: kubectl logs & describe
items.content: `kubectl logs <pod>` shows container logs; `kubectl describe pod <pod>` shows events and status.

items.title: kubectl exec & port-forward
items.content: `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh` opens a shell; `kubectl port-forward <pod> 8080:80` tunnels locally.

items.title: SELECT
items.content: Read rows: `SELECT col1, col2 FROM table WHERE cond ORDER BY col LIMIT n`.

items.title: INSERT
items.content: Add rows: `INSERT INTO table (a, b) VALUES (1, 'x')`.

items.title: UPDATE
items.content: Modify rows: `UPDATE table SET col = val WHERE cond`—always include a WHERE to avoid mass updates.

items.title: DELETE
items.content: Remove rows: `DELETE FROM table WHERE cond`—WHERE is critical, or you delete everything.

items.title: JOIN
items.content: Combine rows from tables: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL—e.g. `SELECT * FROM a JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id`.

items.title: GROUP BY & HAVING
items.content: Aggregate rows by a column with COUNT/SUM/AVG; filter groups with HAVING.

items.title: CREATE TABLE
items.content: Define a new table with columns, types, and constraints: `CREATE TABLE users (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, ...)`.

items.title: ALTER TABLE
items.content: Change an existing table: `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN age INT`.

items.title: CREATE INDEX
items.content: Speed up lookups: `CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email)`—improves reads, slows writes.

items.title: TRANSACTION
items.content: Group statements atomically: `BEGIN; ... COMMIT;` or `ROLLBACK;` to undo on error.

items.title: API
items.content: Application Programming Interface—a contract that lets software components talk to each other.

items.title: HTTP
items.content: HyperText Transfer Protocol—the request/response protocol that powers the web.

items.title: HTML
items.content: HyperText Markup Language—the standard markup that structures web pages.

items.title: CSS
items.content: Cascading Style Sheets—the language that styles and lays out web pages.

items.title: URL
items.content: Uniform Resource Locator—the address used to locate a resource on the web.

items.title: JSON
items.content: JavaScript Object Notation—a lightweight, human-readable data-interchange format.

items.title: XML
items.content: eXtensible Markup Language—a verbose, structured format for data exchange and config.

items.title: YAML
items.content: YAML Ain't Markup Language—a human-friendly data format common in config files.

items.title: CRUD
items.content: Create, Read, Update, Delete—the four basic operations on persistent data.

items.title: REST
items.content: REpresentational State Transfer—an architectural style for stateless web APIs.

items.title: SOAP
items.content: Simple Object Access Protocol—an older, XML-based protocol for web services.

items.title: SDK
items.content: Software Development Kit—a bundle of tools, libraries, and docs for building on a platform.

items.title: IDE
items.content: Integrated Development Environment—an editor with build, debug, and tooling integrated.

items.title: CLI
items.content: Command-Line Interface—a text-based way to interact with programs and the OS.

items.title: GUI
items.content: Graphical User Interface—a visual, point-and-click way to interact with software.

items.title: DOM
items.content: Document Object Model—the tree representation of a web page that scripts manipulate.

items.title: ORM
items.content: Object-Relational Mapping—maps database tables to code objects so you query in your language.

items.title: SQL
items.content: Structured Query Language—the standard language for relational databases.

items.title: CI/CD
items.content: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery—automated build, test, and release pipelines.

items.title: DNS
items.content: Domain Name System—translates domain names into IP addresses.

items.title: TCP/IP
items.content: Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol—the core suite that runs the internet.

items.title: TLS/SSL
items.content: Transport Layer Security / Secure Sockets Layer—encrypts data in transit (HTTPS).

items.title: JWT
items.content: JSON Web Token—a signed token format for stateless authentication.

items.title: CORS
items.content: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing—browser rules controlling cross-origin requests.

items.title: XSS
items.content: Cross-Site Scripting—an attack injecting malicious scripts into web pages.

items.title: CSRF
items.content: Cross-Site Request Forgery—tricks a user's browser into making unwanted authenticated requests.

items.title: DDoS
items.content: Distributed Denial of Service—flooding a service from many sources to take it offline.

items.title: MVC
items.content: Model-View-Controller—a pattern separating data, UI, and control logic.

items.title: MVP
items.content: Minimum Viable Product—the smallest releasable version that delivers value and validates an idea.

items.title: SaaS
items.content: Software as a Service—software delivered over the internet on subscription.

items.title: CDN
items.content: Content Delivery Network—distributed edge servers caching content near users.

items.title: RAM
items.content: Random Access Memory—fast volatile memory holding active programs and data.

items.title: CPU
items.content: Central Processing Unit—the chip that executes program instructions.

items.title: GPU
items.content: Graphics Processing Unit—massively parallel processor for graphics and ML workloads.

items.title: OOP
items.content: Object-Oriented Programming—organizing code around objects with state and behavior.

items.title: DRY
items.content: Don't Repeat Yourself—avoid duplication by having a single source of truth.

items.title: SOLID
items.content: Five OOP design principles for maintainable, flexible object-oriented code.

items.title: ACID
items.content: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability—guarantees of reliable database transactions.

items.title: UUID
items.content: Universally Unique Identifier—a 128-bit globally unique ID.

items.title: LLM
items.content: Large Language Model—an AI model trained on massive text for language tasks.

items.title: Supervised Learning
items.content: Training a model on labeled examples so it learns to map inputs to known outputs.

items.title: Unsupervised Learning
items.content: Finding structure (clusters, patterns) in unlabeled data without predefined targets.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning
items.content: An agent learns by taking actions in an environment and maximizing cumulative reward.

items.title: Gradient Descent
items.content: Optimization that iteratively adjusts model weights in the direction that reduces error.

items.title: Backpropagation
items.content: Algorithm that computes gradients through a neural network to update weights during training.

items.title: Transformer
items.content: Neural architecture using self-attention to process sequences in parallel—the basis of modern LLMs.

items.title: Attention Mechanism
items.content: Lets a model weigh the relevance of different input tokens when producing each output.

items.title: Fine-Tuning
items.content: Adapting a pretrained model to a specific task by training further on a smaller, focused dataset.

items.title: Token
items.content: The unit (word piece) an LLM reads and generates; pricing and context limits are measured in tokens.

items.title: Hallucination
items.content: When an LLM confidently produces false or fabricated information not grounded in data.

items.title: Temperature
items.content: Sampling parameter controlling LLM randomness—low is focused and deterministic, high is creative.

items.title: Context Window
items.content: The maximum number of tokens an LLM can consider at once for input plus output.

items.title: Vector Embedding
items.content: Numeric representation of text or data capturing meaning, enabling similarity search.

items.title: Feature Engineering
items.content: Crafting and selecting input variables that make patterns easier for a model to learn.

items.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
items.content: Balancing underfitting (high bias) against overfitting (high variance) for good generalization.

items.title: Precision vs Recall
items.content: Precision is how many predicted positives are correct; recall is how many actual positives were found.

items.title: Confusion Matrix
items.content: Table of true/false positives and negatives used to evaluate a classifier's performance.

items.title: Epoch & Batch
items.content: An epoch is one full pass over training data; a batch is the subset processed before a weight update.

items.title: Transfer Learning
items.content: Reusing knowledge from a model trained on one task to jump-start learning on a related one.

items.title: CNN
items.content: Convolutional Neural Network—a model specialized for grid data like images using convolution filters.

items.title: RNN & LSTM
items.content: Recurrent networks (and LSTM variants) process sequences by carrying state across time steps.

items.title: Diffusion Model
items.content: Generative model that creates images by iteratively denoising random noise (e.g. Stable Diffusion).

items.title: GAN
items.content: Generative Adversarial Network—a generator and discriminator compete to produce realistic data.

items.title: Agent (AI)
items.content: An LLM-driven system that plans, calls tools, and acts in steps to accomplish a goal autonomously.

items.title: MCP
items.content: Model Context Protocol—an open standard letting AI assistants connect to tools and data sources.

items.title: Authentication vs Authorization
items.content: Authentication verifies who you are; authorization decides what you're allowed to do.

items.title: MFA
items.content: Multi-Factor Authentication adds a second proof (code, device, biometric) beyond a password.

items.title: Salting & Hashing
items.content: Add a unique random salt before hashing passwords so identical passwords don't share a hash.

items.title: Symmetric vs Asymmetric Encryption
items.content: Symmetric uses one shared key; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair for exchange and signing.

items.title: Public Key Infrastructure
items.content: System of certificates and authorities that binds public keys to identities for trust (PKI).

items.title: Zero Trust
items.content: Security model that trusts nothing by default and verifies every request regardless of network location.

items.title: Principle of Least Privilege
items.content: Grant each user or process only the minimum access needed, limiting damage from compromise.

items.title: Man-in-the-Middle
items.content: Attack where a third party secretly intercepts and possibly alters communication between two parties.

items.title: Phishing
items.content: Social-engineering attack tricking users into revealing credentials or installing malware.

items.title: SQL Injection (deep)
items.content: Injecting SQL through unsanitized input to read or modify data; defend with parameterized queries.

items.title: Security Headers
items.content: HTTP headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options) that harden web apps against common attacks.

items.title: Rate Limiting (security)
items.content: Throttle requests to slow brute-force, scraping, and denial-of-service attempts.

items.title: OWASP Top 10 (list)
items.content: The ten most critical web risks: injection, broken access control, crypto failures, misconfig, and more.

items.title: Penetration Testing
items.content: Authorized simulated attack to find and report exploitable vulnerabilities before real attackers do.

items.title: CVE
items.content: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures—a public catalog of known security flaws with unique IDs.

items.title: SPA
items.content: Single-Page Application loads one HTML shell and updates content via JavaScript without full reloads.

items.title: SSR vs CSR
items.content: Server-Side Rendering builds HTML on the server for fast first paint; Client-Side Rendering builds it in the browser.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Process of attaching JavaScript interactivity to server-rendered HTML on the client.

items.title: PWA
items.content: Progressive Web App—a website that installs and works offline like a native app using service workers.

items.title: Service Worker
items.content: Background script that intercepts requests to enable offline caching, push, and background sync.

items.title: Web Components
items.content: Browser standard for reusable, encapsulated custom elements via Shadow DOM and templates.

items.title: Responsive Design
items.content: Layouts that adapt to any screen size using fluid grids, flexible images, and media queries.

items.title: Flexbox & Grid
items.content: CSS layout systems: Flexbox lays out items in one dimension, Grid in two dimensions.

items.title: Critical Rendering Path
items.content: The sequence the browser follows to turn HTML, CSS, and JS into pixels; optimize it for fast paint.

items.title: Core Web Vitals
items.content: Google's UX metrics—LCP (load), INP (interactivity), CLS (visual stability)—that affect ranking.

items.title: Code Splitting
items.content: Breaking a bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand to cut initial JavaScript download.

items.title: State Management
items.content: Patterns and libraries (Redux, Zustand, Signals) for sharing and updating UI state predictably.

items.title: Reactivity
items.content: UI paradigm where the view automatically updates when underlying data changes.

items.title: AJAX
items.content: Asynchronous JavaScript technique to fetch data and update a page without a full reload.

items.title: Cookies vs LocalStorage
items.content: Cookies are sent with every request and good for sessions; localStorage persists data only in the browser.

items.title: Accessibility (a11y)
items.content: Designing apps usable by people with disabilities via semantic HTML, ARIA, contrast, and keyboard support.

items.title: SEO
items.content: Search Engine Optimization—structuring content and metadata so pages rank well in search results.

items.title: Favicon & Meta Tags
items.content: Small page metadata controlling the tab icon, social previews (Open Graph), and SEO description.

items.title: Native vs Hybrid vs Cross-Platform
items.content: Native uses platform languages; hybrid wraps web in a shell; cross-platform (Flutter, RN) compiles one codebase to both.

items.title: Activity & Fragment
items.content: Android building blocks: an Activity is a screen; a Fragment is a reusable portion of UI within it.

items.title: View Controller
items.content: iOS object that manages a screen's views and responds to lifecycle and user events.

items.title: App Lifecycle
items.content: The states an app moves through—foreground, background, suspended—each needing proper handling.

items.title: Push Notifications
items.content: Messages delivered to a device via APNs (iOS) or FCM (Android) even when the app is closed.

items.title: Deep Linking
items.content: URLs that open a specific screen inside an app, enabling sharing and seamless navigation.

items.title: App Store Review
items.content: Approval process Apple and Google run before publishing; plan for guidelines, privacy, and rejections.

items.title: Responsive Layout (mobile)
items.content: Use density-independent units and constraints so UIs scale across phone and tablet sizes.

items.title: Offline-First
items.content: Design that stores data locally and syncs when online, so the app works without connectivity.

items.title: Code Signing
items.content: Cryptographically signing an app build to prove its origin and integrity for distribution.

items.title: Hot Reload
items.content: Apply code changes to a running app instantly without losing state—speeds up mobile/UI development.

items.title: Battery & Resource Optimization
items.content: Minimize wakeups, background work, and network calls so the app preserves battery and data.

items.title: Primary Key vs Foreign Key
items.content: A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table.

items.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
items.content: Read Uncommitted to Serializable—trade consistency for concurrency, controlling dirty/phantom reads.

items.title: OLTP vs OLAP
items.content: OLTP handles many small transactions (apps); OLAP runs complex analytical queries (reporting).

items.title: Materialized View
items.content: A stored, precomputed query result refreshed periodically to speed up expensive reads.

items.title: Stored Procedure
items.content: Precompiled SQL logic stored in the database and invoked by name for reuse and performance.

items.title: Query Optimizer
items.content: Database component that chooses the most efficient execution plan for a query.

items.title: B-Tree vs LSM-Tree
items.content: B-Trees suit read-heavy indexes; LSM-Trees (used in Cassandra, RocksDB) suit write-heavy workloads.

items.title: Connection Limit
items.content: Databases cap concurrent connections; use pooling and queues to stay under it at scale.

items.title: Soft Delete
items.content: Mark rows deleted with a flag instead of removing them, preserving history and enabling recovery.

items.title: Migration
items.content: Versioned, incremental change to a database schema applied consistently across environments.

items.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
items.content: Optimistic assumes no conflict and checks at commit; pessimistic locks rows upfront to block others.

items.title: Time-Series Database
items.content: Database optimized for timestamped data and range queries (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) for metrics and IoT.

items.title: Compiler vs Interpreter
items.content: A compiler translates code to machine code ahead of time; an interpreter executes it line by line.

items.title: Static vs Dynamic Typing
items.content: Static typing checks types at compile time; dynamic typing checks at runtime, trading safety for flexibility.

items.title: Pass by Value vs Reference
items.content: By value copies the data; by reference shares it, so callee changes affect the caller.

items.title: Stack vs Heap Memory
items.content: The stack stores fast, short-lived call data; the heap stores dynamically allocated, longer-lived objects.

items.title: Closures
items.content: A function bundled with references to its surrounding scope, letting it remember variables after that scope ends.

items.title: Higher-Order Function
items.content: A function that takes other functions as arguments or returns one—core to functional programming.

items.title: Currying
items.content: Transforming a multi-argument function into a chain of single-argument functions.

items.title: Recursion vs Iteration
items.content: Recursion solves problems by self-calls; iteration uses loops—each trades clarity, stack use, and speed.

items.title: Mutability
items.content: Whether a value can be changed after creation; immutable data is safer for concurrency and caching.

items.title: Type Coercion
items.content: Implicit conversion between types (e.g. string to number) that can cause subtle bugs in loose languages.

items.title: Exception Handling
items.content: Structured way to catch and recover from runtime errors using try/catch/finally.

items.title: Reflection
items.content: Ability of a program to inspect and modify its own structure and behavior at runtime.

items.title: Serialization
items.content: Converting an object into a storable/transmittable format (JSON, protobuf) and back again.

items.title: Encapsulation
items.content: OOP principle of hiding internal state and exposing behavior through a controlled interface.

items.title: Abstraction
items.content: Hiding complex details behind a simpler interface so callers work at a higher level.

items.title: Coupling vs Cohesion
items.content: Low coupling (few dependencies) and high cohesion (focused responsibility) make systems maintainable.

items.title: Technical Debt
items.content: The future cost of choosing a quick solution now over a better one; pay it down before it compounds.

items.title: Refactoring
items.content: Improving code's internal structure without changing its external behavior, backed by tests.

items.title: Regular Expression
items.content: A pattern language for matching, searching, and replacing text—powerful but easy to overuse.

items.title: Bitwise Operations
items.content: Operate directly on bits (AND, OR, XOR, shifts) for flags, masks, and performance-critical code.

items.title: Profiling
items.content: Measuring where a program spends time and memory to find the real bottlenecks before optimizing.

items.title: Benchmarking
items.content: Running repeatable workloads to quantify performance and compare implementations objectively.

items.title: Time Complexity
items.content: How an algorithm's runtime grows with input size, expressed in Big O notation.

items.title: Space Complexity
items.content: How an algorithm's memory use grows with input size, also expressed in Big O.

items.title: Amortized Complexity
items.content: Average cost per operation over a sequence, smoothing out occasional expensive operations.

items.title: Cache Hit Ratio
items.content: Fraction of requests served from cache; a higher ratio means lower latency and backend load.

items.title: Lazy vs Eager Evaluation
items.content: Lazy computes values only when needed; eager computes immediately—affects performance and memory.

items.title: Memory Footprint
items.content: The amount of RAM a program uses; smaller footprints scale better and reduce cost.

items.title: Throttling vs Debouncing
items.content: Throttling limits calls to once per interval; debouncing waits for a pause—both reduce work.

items.title: Hot Path
items.content: The most frequently executed code path; optimizing it yields the biggest performance gains.

items.title: Prefer async over blocking
items.content: Use async I/O so threads aren't tied up waiting on network or disk, boosting throughput.

items.title: Validate at the boundary
items.content: Sanitize and validate data as it enters your system so the core can trust it everywhere else.

items.title: Use enums over strings
items.content: Replace stringly-typed values with enums so the compiler catches typos and invalid states.

items.title: Return errors, don't swallow them
items.content: Never catch an exception and ignore it; handle, log, or rethrow so failures stay visible.

items.title: Write the test list first
items.content: Before coding, jot down the cases you must handle; it clarifies requirements and prevents gaps.

items.title: Keep config out of code
items.content: Externalize URLs, limits, and toggles so behavior changes without redeploying or recompiling.

items.title: Prefer pure functions
items.content: Functions without side effects are easy to test, cache, and reason about—favor them where you can.

items.title: Measure twice, deploy once
items.content: Validate in staging with production-like data before shipping; surprises cost more in prod.

items.title: Add timeouts everywhere
items.content: Every external call should have a timeout so a slow dependency can't cascade into a system hang.

items.title: Use structured logging
items.content: Log JSON with consistent fields so logs are searchable and machine-parseable, not free-text blobs.

items.title: Paginate and stream big results
items.content: Never load millions of rows into memory; page or stream them to stay within limits.

items.title: Guard against integer overflow
items.content: Be mindful of numeric limits in IDs, counters, and money math—use the right types and checks.

items.title: Localize from day one
items.content: Wrap user-facing text and format dates/numbers per locale early; retrofitting i18n is painful.

items.title: Document the why, not the what
items.content: Comments should explain intent and tradeoffs; the code already shows what it does.

items.title: Automate dependency scanning
items.content: Run tools like Dependabot to flag vulnerable packages and keep your supply chain secure.

items.content: Cloud-native reverse proxy and load balancer that auto-discovers services and manages TLS.

items.content: Hub and libraries (Transformers) for sharing, running, and fine-tuning ML models.

items.title: Loki

items.title: OpenTelemetry

items.title: Cloudflare
items.content: Global CDN, DNS, DDoS protection, and edge-compute platform for fast, secure sites.

items.title: AWS

items.content: Python data-validation library using type hints to parse and validate structured data.

items.content: End-to-end typesafe APIs for TypeScript apps without schemas or code generation.

items.content: Microsoft's ORM for .NET enabling LINQ queries and migrations against databases.

items.title: COBOL

items.content: Microsoft's object-oriented shell and scripting language for automating Windows and cloud admin.

items.content: Schema Definition Language used to declare GraphQL types, queries, and mutations.

items.content: Generate a migration, define up/down changes, run it on a copy first, then apply and verify in each environment.

items.content: Issue a signed token on login, store it client-side, send it as a Bearer header, and verify it on protected routes.

items.content: Install both, add config files, resolve conflicts with eslint-config-prettier, and run them in a pre-commit hook.

items.content: Write Dockerfiles per service, define them in docker-compose.yml with networks and volumes, then `docker compose up`.

items.title: Write integration tests
items.content: Spin up a test database, seed data, exercise real endpoints, assert responses, and tear down cleanly each run.

items.title: Set up a monorepo

items.title: Profile and fix a slow endpoint
items.content: Reproduce under load, profile to find the bottleneck (often a query), add an index or cache, then re-measure.

items.title: SSR

items.title: BDD

items.title: DDD
items.content: Domain-Driven Design—modeling software around the business domain and a shared language.

items.title: KISS

items.title: YAGNI
items.content: You Aren't Gonna Need It—don't build features until they're actually required.

items.title: WYSIWYG
items.content: What You See Is What You Get—editors that render content as it will finally appear.

items.title: VPN

items.content: File Transfer Protocol (and its secure SSH variant) for moving files between hosts.

items.title: RPC

items.title: SDK vs API
items.content: An SDK is a full toolkit for building on a platform; an API is the interface you call.

items.title: WebGL / WebGPU
items.content: Browser APIs for GPU-accelerated 2D/3D graphics; WebGPU is the modern successor to WebGL.

items.title: IoT

items.title: ROI
items.content: Return on Investment—the value gained relative to the cost, used to prioritize work.

items.title: npm run

items.title: npx
items.content: Run a package binary without installing it globally: `npx create-react-app my-app`.

items.title: yarn / pnpm
items.content: Alternative Node package managers; `pnpm install` is fast and disk-efficient via a content-addressable store.

items.title: pip install
items.content: Install Python packages: `pip install <pkg>`; freeze versions with `pip freeze > requirements.txt`.
